title: The Alphabet
subtitle: Twenty-four letters borrowed from Latin plus four Germanic holdovers.
objectives: Recognize the twenty-four basic letters of Old English orthography.
Distinguish the four additional letters (æ, þ, ð, ƿ) from their Latin counterparts.
Understand that Old English uses no j, no v, and no q in native words.
Begin to associate the written forms with the sounds they represent.

sections.heading: Where we begin
sections.body: Old English is written in the Latin alphabet, but not quite the Latin alphabet you know. The scribes who first put Anglo-Saxon speech to parchment borrowed the twenty-three letters of Latin (there was no w in Latin) and added four more to capture the sounds Latin lacked. You will recognize twenty of the letters at once. The other four require attention.

sections.heading: What is missing
sections.body: Three letters of modern English are absent from Old English orthography: j, q, and v. The j did not exist as a separate letter in Latin (it was a variant form of i). The v was a variant form of u. The q appeared in Latin but was not needed for Germanic words; Old English used c and cw where Latin used q. When you see a j in a modern edition of an Old English text, the manuscript had an i.

letters.name: a
letters.note: Short or long. Short as in 'cat,' long as in 'father.'

letters.name: b
letters.note: As in modern English 'boy.'

letters.name: c
letters.note: Always hard [k] before a, o, u, consonants. Before e, i, y it palatalized to [tʃ] (as in 'church').

letters.name: d
letters.note: As in 'dog.'

letters.name: e
letters.note: Short as in 'met,' long as in French 'été.'

letters.name: f
letters.note: Voiceless [f] at the start or end of a word; voiced [v] between vowels.

letters.name: g
letters.note: Complex. Stop [ɡ] initially before a, o, u. Fricative [ɣ] (like Spanish 'lago') between vowels. Palatalized [j] (like 'yes') before e, i, y.

letters.name: h
letters.note: Aspirate [h] before a vowel. Guttural [x] (like German 'ach') before consonants or at word-end.

letters.name: i
letters.note: Short or long. As in 'sit' or 'machine.'

letters.name: l
letters.note: As in 'let.'

letters.name: m
letters.note: As in 'man.'

letters.name: n
letters.note: As in 'no.'

letters.name: o
letters.note: Short or long. Short as in 'lot,' long as in 'boat.'

letters.name: p
letters.note: As in 'pin.'

letters.name: r
letters.note: Trilled, as in Scottish or Spanish.

letters.name: s
letters.note: Voiceless [s] at the start or end. Voiced [z] between vowels.

letters.name: t
letters.note: As in 'top.'

letters.name: u
letters.note: Short or long. As in 'put' or 'boot.'

letters.name: x
letters.note: Rare. Represents [ks] as in 'axe.'

letters.name: y
letters.note: Front rounded vowel. Like German ü in 'über' or French u in 'tu.'

sections.heading: The four additional letters
sections.body: Four letters appear in Old English that do not appear in the modern English alphabet. Three are borrowed from the runic alphabet (þ, ð, ƿ); one is a Latin ligature (æ). You must learn to recognize them and reproduce them. Modern printed editions retain them; modern typists often substitute th for þ and ð, w for ƿ, and ae for æ, but we will not. The letters matter.

letters.name: ash
letters.note: The vowel in modern 'cat' or 'hat.' A ligature of a and e.

letters.name: thorn
letters.note: Both voiceless 'th' (as in 'thin') and voiced 'th' (as in 'this'). Scribes used þ and ð interchangeably.

letters.name: eth
letters.note: Identical in sound to þ. Scribes chose between them by preference or manuscript tradition.

letters.name: wynn
letters.note: The sound of modern 'w.' Looks like p but is not. From the rune *wynn*.

sections.heading: Why the old letters matter
sections.body: Replacing æ with ae, þ with th, and ƿ with w makes Old English look like modern English with strange spelling. It is not. It is a different language. The letters remind you of that. When you see þæt, you see an Old English word. When you see 'thaet,' you see a transliteration. We read the language, not the transliteration.

sections.heading: Self-check
sections.instructions: Cover the right column. Name each letter and its sound.

items.answer: front rounded vowel, like German ü
[k] before a, o, u; [tʃ] before e, i, y
stop, fricative, or palatal depending on position
[h] before vowels, [x] before consonants or at word-end

items.prompt: What three letters of modern English are absent from Old English?
Why are þ and ð both present if they represent the same sounds?
items.answer: Scribal tradition. Different scriptoria preferred one or the other; some used both.

sections.heading: First words
sections.instructions: You can read these now. Sound them out before checking the audio.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 1.2 covers the four special letters in detail and introduces the concept of vowel length. After that you will begin reading your first Old English sentences.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark complete when you can name all twenty-eight letters (24 + 4) and their sounds without hesitation.
